title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
description: Brute force to optimized: a flat set of words versus a trie sharing common prefixes as a single path.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Implement a Trie (prefix tree) with insert(word) (insert a word), search(word) (return whether the exact word was inserted), and startsWith(prefix) (return whether any inserted word starts with this prefix).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A sequence of insert, search, startsWith calls"],["Output","search/startsWith return booleans"],["Goal","O(word length) per operation, independent of the number of words stored"],["Constraints","Up to 3*10^4 calls, words up to 2000 characters"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Prefix tree\" explicitly named","A tree where each node represents one character position, shared across all words with the same prefix"],["\"Insert, exact search, prefix search\"","Each node needs children (by next character) and an end-of-word marker"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Words sharing a common prefix can share the same path of nodes in the tree, one node per character. An "end of word" marker at a node distinguishes "prefix seen" from "an actual complete word ends here."

blocks.title: Analogy: A Branching Signpost Tree for Words
blocks.text: Picture a branching signpost system where each fork represents one letter, and words sharing a beginning share the same forks. Following a word letter by letter down this branching path either leads to a "complete word" marker or simply confirms the prefix exists without necessarily being a full word itself.

blocks.caption: Words sharing a prefix share the same path of nodes; an end-of-word flag marks complete words

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: insert("apple"), search("apple"), search("app"), startsWith("app"), insert("app"), search("app")
Results: null, true, false, true, null, true. "app" is a prefix but not inserted as a word until the second insert.
5. How Should We Think?

Before storing all words in a flat list or set (which supports exact search but requires scanning everything for prefix queries), notice that a tree where each node represents one character position, shared across words with common prefixes, answers BOTH search and startsWith in O(word length).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: insert(word) walks the tree one character at a time, creating new nodes only where the path does not already exist, then marks the final node as "end of word."

Observation 2: search(word) walks the same path; if it cannot complete the full path, the word was never inserted; if it completes the path, the word exists only if the final node is marked "end of word."

Observation 3: startsWith(prefix) is nearly identical to search, but does NOT require the final node to be marked as end of word, just that the path exists.

Observation 4: Since each operation only ever walks a path of length equal to the word/prefix, none of these operations depend on the total number of words stored.
This leads to a tree of character nodes: insert walks/creates the path and marks the end; search walks the path and checks the end marker; startsWith walks the path only.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store all inserted words in a set. search() is then an O(1) set lookup, but startsWith() requires scanning every stored word to check if any begins with the prefix.
Why the code is written this way

items: A set gives O(1) exact-word search directly.
startsWith requires scanning every word, costing O(total words times prefix length), independent of how many words actually share the prefix.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(word length) for insert/search, O(total words times prefix length) for startsWith.
Space: O(total characters across all words).
Limitation: a trie answers startsWith in O(prefix length), independent of the number of stored words, by sharing prefix paths directly.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Build a tree where each node represents a character position, with children keyed by the next character. insert() walks/creates this path, marking the final node as end-of-word. search() walks the same path and checks the end marker. startsWith() walks the path without requiring the end marker, since only prefix existence matters.
Maintain a root trie node. insert/search/startsWith all walk character by character, creating nodes as needed (insert only) or failing early if a character is missing (search/startsWith).
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for insert("apple"), then search("app")

blocks.content: {"headers":["Call","Path walked","Result"],"rows":[["insert(\"apple\")","creates a-p-p-l-e, marks e as end","-"],["search(\"app\")","walks a-p-p, but this node is NOT marked end","false"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

Since words sharing a prefix follow the SAME path in the trie, checking prefix existence only ever requires walking that one path, independent of how many words (or how many OTHER words) were inserted. The end-of-word marker correctly distinguishes "this exact word was inserted" from "this is merely a prefix of some longer inserted word."

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(word/prefix length) for all three operations.
Space: O(total characters across all UNIQUE prefixes, shared where possible).

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Implement Trie (Prefix Tree) is the foundational data structure for all prefix-based string problems, sharing common prefixes as a single path.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting the end-of-word marker, causing search() to incorrectly return true for mere prefixes.
Confusing search() (needs the end marker) with startsWith() (does not).

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["Empty string operations","Handled correctly since the loop simply does not execute."],["Searching for a word that is only ever a prefix of another","Correctly returns false via the end-of-word check."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating the end-of-word marker's purpose (distinguishing "prefix exists" from "exact word exists") clarifies the key subtlety of this structure.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "efficient prefix-based storage and lookup", think: a trie, sharing common prefixes as one path, with an end-of-word marker.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you also support deletion of a word?
How would you extend this to support wildcard search (Design Add and Search Words Data Structure)?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Every trie-based problem in this category builds directly on this foundational structure.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: A flat set costs O(1) for search but O(n) for prefix queries; a trie costs O(length) for all operations, the standard foundational solution.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a trie (prefix tree), sharing common prefixes as a single path of character nodes.
Core Idea: insert creates the path and marks the end; search checks the path plus the end marker; startsWith checks only the path.
Time: O(1)/O(n) for a flat set, O(length) for all operations in a trie.
Space: O(total characters) for both, but a trie shares common prefixes.
Most Important Observation: shared prefixes mean prefix queries cost only O(prefix length), independent of the number of stored words.
Interview Difficulty: a foundational, must-know data structure for string problems.
One line memory trick: one node per character, shared prefixes, end-of-word marker.
